what: Cardan velocity ripple and differential subtraction. This 300-piece simulation experiment uses two equal-angle Cardan joints, a symmetric differential and a pointer. The second joint is quarter-turn misphased, so its speed variation adds to the first joint's variation. The pointer shows a periodic angular waveform; no elastic wave travels through the model. Two bent, misphased Cardan joints create speed ripple. A differential reveals it as passive pointer motion. 298 placements plus two inferred crosses: 300 physical pieces.
try: Choose WaveMaker — the example loads its Blocks program automatically. Reset the model to its saved starting position, then Run. The program makes four slow pointer cycles at 30°/s, four faster cycles at 60°/s, then reverses through eight cycles before holding at the start target.
Reset, then choose WaveMaker Control and Run the same program. The second joint's forks are correctly phased, so the output pointer nearly cancels the ripple.
Compare the reference shaft, the Cardan output shaft, the differential carrier and pointer. The outer shafts average one turn for one turn in both versions, but their instantaneous motion differs.
why: A bent universal joint does not turn its output at a constant instantaneous speed. Equal bends cancel that variation when the middle forks are aligned. A quarter-turn phase shift makes the second variation reinforce the first. The differential converts the two signed side-shaft motions into their average, and a 16-tooth rim driving an 8-tooth pinion doubles the carrier angle while reversing its sign.
matters: Universal joints let shafts transmit rotation across an angle. Fork phase matters when two joints are combined: one-to-one average turns do not guarantee constant instantaneous speed. A differential follows the arithmetic mean of its equal side gears' signed angles.
question: Both versions turn their outer shafts by nearly the same average amount. Why does the main pointer rock while the control pointer stays almost still?
answer: The quarter-turn phase of the main model makes the two Cardan angle variations add. The correctly phased control makes the second joint undo the first joint's variation. The differential and 16:8 takeoff reveal that difference at the pointer.
further: From the 48–64–80 shaft-center triangle, cos β=0.8 and β≈36.87°. The ideal misphased pointer law has 25.3608° peak-to-peak stroke every 180° of reference-shaft rotation; the hosted trace measures about 25.50° over its full program.

The LDraw file has 298 explicit placements. Add the two required inferred universal-joint crosses for 300 physical pieces. The experiment uses one motor on port A; all shafts and the pointer are passive.
The Blocks program is finite and includes slow, fast, reverse and guarded hold stages. Reset to the saved starting pose before every run. Tested simulation speeds are 30 and 60 degrees per second.
These results are from a native mechanism simulation. They do not establish physical buildability, torque capacity, friction, backlash, real-world swept clearance, or hardware firmware behavior.
formula: β=acos(0.8). For the 90°-misphased double Cardan, δ(θ)=atan2(sin²β·sinθ·cosθ, cos²β·cos²θ+sin²θ). The symmetric differential gives 2·carrier=reference+ripple; the 16T:8T external takeoff gives pointer=−2·carrier=δ. The correctly phased control ideally has δ=0.
